title: seva as vocation
hook: a great ascetic is sent to a market stall to learn dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation at Yudhishthira's great sacrifice: the guest honored first took the job of washing feet at the door. Which unchosen job did you picture taking? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION.` · `THE JOB AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A man stands in the forest so still, for so long, that a pair of birds builds a nest in his matted hair. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. His name is Jajali, an ascetic, and he doesn't move. The birds lay their eggs. The eggs hatch. He stays still until the chicks grow wings, fly off, and stop coming back. Then a thought arrives, and it's a proud one: who in the world is my equal in dharma? An unseen voice answers. Not you, Jajali. There's a merchant in Varanasi named Tuladhara, and you are not his equal. Today, seva as vocation, taught from behind a shop counter.
screen: `BIRDS NEST IN HIS HAIR.` → `WHO IS MY EQUAL?` → `A MERCHANT IN VARANASI.`

segments.voice: So Jajali goes to Varanasi, and finds him: a trader, selling goods in the market. Before Jajali can say a word, Tuladhara greets him and tells him his own story. The stillness, the birds, the proud thought, the voice. Jajali asks the obvious question. You sell things for a living. How do you know any of this? Tuladhara's answer, in paraphrase, is the teaching. He says he knows the ancient dharma, and he names it plainly. It is friendship toward all beings, and a way of living that harms them as little as it can. He earns his bread by trade, and he keeps it honest. He doesn't cheat on the weight. He doesn't flatter or run anyone down to make a sale. He holds the same even scale for everyone who comes to his counter. Even his name fits. In Sanskrit, a tula is a balance, and Tuladhara can be heard as the one who holds the scales. In this story, the scale on the counter and the evenness in his mind turn out to be one practice. Now notice who's teaching whom. The great ascetic, with birds in his hair, walks all the way to a market to learn from a man who weighs things for a living. The Mahabharata doesn't tell Jajali to open a shop. It doesn't call his years in the forest a waste. It says dharma was already sitting at that counter, in an honest weight handed to a customer Tuladhara might never see again. That's one face of seva as vocation. Not service added on top of a job, like a shift you volunteer for on the weekend. Service as the way the job itself gets done. A scale held level serves every buyer who trusts it, whether or not anyone notices.
screen: `TULADHARA TELLS JAJALI HIS OWN STORY.` · `FRIENDSHIP TOWARD ALL BEINGS.` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SCALES.` · `DHARMA AT THE SHOP COUNTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the scales level. Sit comfortably, and rest your hands palm up on your knees, like the two pans of a balance. Let the breath come and go on its own. Now bring to mind one exchange waiting for you today: a sale, a report, a favor, a reply. Notice where you'd be tempted to tip it a little: a corner cut, a bit of flattery, a shortcut no one would catch. Feel which hand wants to dip. Then let both hands rest evenly again, and breathe there. The work is the same work, weighed true. If you pray, you can offer that exchange to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Seva as vocation. Service done through the work itself, the way Tuladhara served everyone who trusted his scales.
Your line: seva as vocation. Today, in one ordinary exchange, a reply, an invoice, a handoff, give the full measure, the way you'd want it weighed for you. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers sometimes retell the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali from the Mahabharata to show that honest work in an ordinary trade can itself be a way of dharma.

match.prompt: the merchant and the ascetic — tap the pairs.
pairs: the ascetic with birds in his hair
a balance, a pair of scales

myth: Tuladhara tells Jajali to leave the forest and open a shop
the story doesn't say that. it shows dharma already at work behind an honest counter.
Tuladhara knows Jajali's story before Jajali tells it
he greets him and recounts the stillness, the birds and the proud thought.
in the story, the ascetic teaches the merchant
it's the other way around: Jajali walks to Varanasi to learn from Tuladhara.

fork.setup: you're Jajali. birds have just raised their chicks in your hair, and a voice says a merchant knows dharma better than you. what do you do?
options: dismiss it: a shopkeeper can't know dharma.
go to Varanasi and find him.
stand still even longer to prove the voice wrong.
fork.reveal: he goes to the market, and the merchant greets him with his own story. the teacher he needs is behind a counter.

original.note: Sanskrit tulādhāra, the one who holds the scales: the merchant of Varanasi who teaches Jajali dharma in the Mahabharata.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy people leave ordinary work behind.
what it means: in the Mahabharata, a great ascetic is sent to a merchant's counter to learn dharma.
what a scholar hears: the Tuladhara–Jajali dialogue in the Shanti Parva, where an even scale for all and friendship toward all beings are named as dharma.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Moksha-dharma section), the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali

notes: Day 5 of the 'seva as vocation' block (1208–1213). Days 1208–1211 were not on disk when this was written; check that the Tuladhara story is not repeated in them. The review is written generically for that reason.

Tuladhara–Jajali: Shanti Parva, chapters around 261–264 depending on edition (Ganguli numbering differs from the Critical Edition). Confirm details as retold: birds nesting in Jajali's matted hair while he stood still, the chicks growing and leaving, his pride, the voice from the sky naming Tuladhara of Varanasi, Tuladhara recounting Jajali's story on arrival.

Tuladhara's teaching paraphrased as friendship toward all beings, living with the least harm, honest trade, no flattery or blame for gain, and an even scale for all. Confirm this is a fair summary; the dialogue goes on to criticize animal sacrifice, which is left out here.
Name glossed as tulā (balance) + dhāra (holder). Standard Sanskrit; confirm.
No numbers or dates are stated.

Editor pass: review now picks up day 1211 (Krishna washing feet at the Rajasuya) instead of a generic line; the stale note about 1208–1211 being off disk is superseded (they are on disk and do not use Tuladhara).
